assigned.title: release clears the implementation base, or a re-claim inherits a stale one
assigned.acceptance: ai:release clears implementationBaseSha, so a task returned to an unowned queue and later re-claimed records the base of the round that actually implements it. OBSERVED, not hypothesised: PL-0710 was claimed and started at 33195d593695618b779ab6c97a50817a2694e8df, released with nothing written when its implementing agent was terminated, and re-claimed at HEAD 20edec3aa3f33dbd58aa405d1210f56ce54c207f -- and start reported 'started from 33195d593695', preserving the stale base rather than capturing HEAD. CLAUDE.md says implementationBaseSha is the exact lower bound of the first review range and that the range validator refuses a base that is either wider or narrower, so a preserved base makes the published window wider than the implementation. The rule release already follows is the argument: it discards gate results because 'evidence belongs to one implementation round under one owner', and a base is evidence of where that round began. Required: release clears the base, and ai:unblock is checked for the same defect and fixed if it has it; a scenario in scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs claims, releases, re-claims at a different HEAD and asserts the second base is the second HEAD, because this defect is invisible until exactly that sequence occurs; and the fix must NOT let start overwrite a base on an ordinary re-start of a task that was never released, since that is the falsification --reconcile-existing exists to prevent. Do NOT hand-edit any existing task's recorded base as part of this work; PL-0703 was blocked for that move and the historical records stay as they are.
assigned.notes: Found 2026-09-20 by the lead while re-claiming PL-0710. The harm in that instance was bounded and is recorded rather than repaired: 20edec3 touches only control/ and coordination/ and NOTHING under PL-0710's allowedPaths, so base..HEAD is one commit wider in count but identical in reviewed-surface content. The record is imprecise, not false about what changed.

unit.evidence: node scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs exit 0, 69 scenarios (67 before; scenario 9bd with seven arms and 9be are new). node scripts/test-validate-repo.mjs exit 0, 16 groups. npm run test:scripts exit 0 end to end -- 38 env, 69 control plane, 16 validate-repo, 35 dispatcher. npm run repo:validate exit 0. npm run ai:validate exit 0, 64 tasks, with 13 warnings ALL PRE-EXISTING (stale provenance windows on PL-0104/0501/0105/0706/PL-AI-0005 and three preferredAgent lane mismatches); validate is unchanged by this work. turbo was deliberately not run: this change is outside every workspace. RED, and it is a VALUE red rather than a missing export -- the behaviour existed and returned the wrong value: 'AssertionError: a base that describes nothing under the reviewed surface must not outlive the round that failed to write anything, actual 39c992a5..., expected undefined'. THE REGRESSION WAS MUTATION-CHECKED EIGHT WAYS AND ONE SURVIVED THE FIRST PASS: using currentCommitSha() instead of realHeadSha() meant the rule that an env var must not be able to redefine HEAD and discard a provenance field was documented in a comment and ENFORCED BY NOTHING; a LIBERTY_COMMIT_SHA decoy was added to arm A and it now dies. I RE-RAN ONE MUTATION MYSELF rather than take the table on trust, and chose the one that matters most -- clear-always, which is exactly what this task's acceptance originally asked for: planted, node scripts/test-ai-control-plane.mjs exits 1 with an AssertionError; restored, 69 scenarios pass. So the regression specifically distinguishes the delivered design from the one I asked for. The other seven mutants reported killed cover keep-always, unblock left unwired, provenance left behind on a clear, failing open when git cannot answer, start overwriting any base, and start overwriting only out of REVIEW.

assigned.acceptanceDisputedByImplementation: THE ACCEPTANCE ASKED FOR SOMETHING THE IMPLEMENTATION REFUSED TO BUILD, AND THE ACCEPTANCE IS LEFT STANDING RATHER THAN REWRITTEN TO MATCH WHAT WAS BUILT. I wrote 'ai:release clears implementationBaseSha'. The implementer built something else and gave the argument: the two failure directions are NOT SYMMETRIC. Always keeping the base is wrong in the PL-0710 case -- it is an unreconciled reconciliation, reaching the end state --reconcile-existing exists for while publishing none of the window, count or reason it demands. But ALWAYS CLEARING is wrong in the case PL-0710 was not: a release mid-implementation with committed work hands the next round a base at the new HEAD, so the first review range BEGINS AFTER COMMITTED CODE. A wide base is visible to a reviewer who can interrogate it; A NARROW ONE IS INVISIBLE, and narrow is the direction that lets unreviewed work reach DONE. My acceptance would have shipped a safety regression. WHAT WAS BUILT: the base survives a queue return exactly while base..HEAD still changes something under the task's REVIEWED surface -- the predicate assertReconcilableBase already relies on, not a new idea -- and where the base is kept the release event publishes preservedBaseSurfaceChangedFileCount, so preservation becomes a RECORDED FINDING rather than the silence my objection was actually about. It fails towards keeping: no git, unresolvable HEAD, base absent from the checkout or a failed diff all keep the base and name which, because dropping a published base on an unverified guess is the move this area exists to refuse. Also unlike the original ask: a task whose base was dropped can now legitimately be reconciled by the round that follows, which a released task previously never could. I ALSO FILED THIS TASK ON A FALSE PREMISE and that is recorded too: the comment at ai-control-plane.mjs:1475 documented preservation as deliberate, and I found it only after filing. It was kept and narrowed rather than deleted -- it is still true, because a reconciled base always has committed work behind it and so is never the base that gets dropped. gpt-architect should judge the delivered design against this note, not against my original clause.

assigned.title: A property suite gets a timeout of its own, not vitest's default
assigned.acceptance: packages/contracts declares its own vitest testTimeout, with the reason for the value written down, so its fast-check property suite is not running against a default it can exhaust under load. THIS CLOSES AN OPEN ITEM RATHER THAN OPENING ONE. Round 52 recorded a single observed-but-unreproduced failure in stream-candidate.property.test.ts and the lead could not reproduce it across ten seeds; the PL-0710 part-A work reproduced it deterministically and it was never seed-dependent. It is CONCURRENCY-dependent: the box has 2 cores, turbo's default concurrency is 10, the new @liberty/net-policy package takes the graph from 18 test tasks to 20, and 'refuses a licence endpoint that is not https, whatever else it is' -- which runs in 1.73s standalone -- measured 5.4s and 7.4s under that graph against vitest's 5000ms default. Characterised rather than re-rolled: the same tree at --concurrency=4 passes, and the same tree filtered to 19 tasks at default concurrency passes. Required: the timeout is justified against the suite's measured standalone cost and the headroom a loaded machine needs, not picked round; the config explains that a property suite's cost is a function of run count and machine load rather than of the code under test, so a default sized for unit tests is the wrong instrument; and NOTHING ABOUT THE PROPERTY ITSELF IS WEAKENED -- not the run count, not the generators, not an assertion. Raising a timeout to hide a genuinely slow property would be the same mistake one level out, so if the suite is slow for a reason the code should answer for, say so instead. Out of scope: a turbo concurrency cap, which is a CLI flag rather than a turbo.json key and is a CI decision.
assigned.notes: Found 2026-09-20 during PL-0710 part A. The failing command is npx turbo run test --force at turbo's default concurrency, reproduced 2 of 2. packages/contracts has no vitest.config.ts at all today. packages/media-engine/vitest.config.ts is the house precedent for a package-local config that exists to keep a machine-dependent assertion out of the incidental run, and its header states the reasoning this task should follow.

unit.evidence: npx turbo run test --force AT TURBO'S DEFAULT CONCURRENCY, exit 0, 20 of 20 tasks and 0 cached, 2565 passed 1 skipped. That is the command that matters, because it is the one that was failing. npx vitest run --root packages/contracts alone: 8 files, 202 passed. THE RED IS THE SUBAGENT'S, NOT MINE, AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The agent that found this reproduced the failure two times out of two at default concurrency -- 'Test timed out in 5000ms' on 'refuses a licence endpoint that is not https, whatever else it is' -- and characterised it rather than re-rolling: 2 cores, turbo default concurrency 10, the new net-policy package taking the graph from 18 test tasks to 20, that test measured at 5.4s and 7.4s under the graph against a 1.76s standalone cost for the whole 31-test file. The same tree passed at --concurrency=4 and passed at default concurrency filtered to 19 tasks. I THEN RAN THE RED DIRECTION MYSELF AND IT DID NOT REPRODUCE: with this file removed, the same command on the same tree exited 0. So this is NOT a demonstrated red-to-green repair, and the config comment now says that in terms. It is headroom for a suite measured to be running at roughly a third of the budget it was held to, with no margin, which is a latent fragility whether or not it fires on a given afternoon. Round 52's single unexplained failure in this same suite is BEST EXPLAINED by this and is not thereby proven to be it; that item stays open rather than being closed on a hypothesis. Nothing about the property was weakened -- run count, generators and assertions are untouched, and the only file changed is a new packages/contracts/vitest.config.ts.

recommended.title: Contract module boundaries
recommended.acceptance: Shared vocabularies live in their own leaf modules, domain contracts live in one module each, index.ts is a re-export-only compatibility barrel rather than the authoritative public surface, and a wildcard exports map lets a new domain contract be added without touching package metadata or the barrel; no cycle-driven z.lazy remains and structural regressions prove the boundary rather than merely reflecting it; no schema behaviour changes
